Sequential Certification of Threshold Decisions in Rare-Event Risk Prediction

Hui-Mean Foo    Yuan-chin Ivan Chang ††thanks: Corresponding author: Yuan-chin Ivan Chang, Institute of Statistical Science, Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan. Email: ycchang@sinica.edu.tw Affiliation: Institute of Statistical Science, Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan
September 1, 2026
Abstract

Rare clinical outcomes pose a difficulty deeper than ordinary class imbalance: a penalized logistic model can return finite, stable-looking coefficients before the data support a reliable threshold decision. We formulate the accrual question as decision-targeted sequential certification. On a prespecified finite monitoring schedule and target set, asymptotic prediction bands are adjusted for simultaneous coverage, and certification is assessed only among profiles that might be referred, so that a large low-risk majority cannot trigger an uninformative stop. Under the working rare-event logistic model and stated regularity conditions, each certified decision is asymptotically model-conditionally correct with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha over the schedule, and the effective information scales with the number of genuine events. Simulations and a US linked birth/infant-death application illustrate the gap between a model that is merely estimable and one whose decisions are certifiable: the whole-population rule stopped while more than half of referral-relevant profiles remained ambiguous, whereas the decision-targeted rule did not certify by the 300,000-birth horizon despite stable temporal validation. Regularization makes a rare-event model estimable but does not substitute for genuine rare-event information.

Keywords: rare events; logistic regression; sequential analysis; simultaneous inference; risk prediction; clinical decision threshold

1 Introduction

Rare medical outcomes pose a problem more fundamental than ordinary class imbalance. When a clinical risk model is updated as patients accrue, only a few events may have been observed early on; a penalized logistic fit can then return finite coefficients and apparently stable probabilities while the data still carry too little genuine event information to support a precise clinical decision. The question of interest is therefore not merely whether a classifier discriminates well at a fixed sample size, but when enough genuine information has accumulated for a calibrated risk prediction, and the clinical decision taken from it at a prespecified threshold, to be made with controlled uncertainty. Posed this way, estimation and classification are one problem: the data yield a fitted risk p^n​(x)\widehat{p}_{n}(x), which yields a decision at a threshold τ\tau, which is either certified or deferred until more patients accrue.

Several ingredients of this problem have been studied, but separately. Many sequential methods have been developed for logistic regression models, and most target the precision of coefficient estimates through the information matrix, for example, fixed-precision sequential inference for logistic regression [1, 3]. In addition, rare-event logistic regression and small-event bias have been studied extensively [10], and Firth and separation-robust fitting address the divergence of the ordinary maximum likelihood estimator, though probability calibration under rare events still requires care [11, 12, 13]. Prediction-model sample-size work shows that raw events-per-variable rules are inadequate and that calibration and overall performance matter [15], and machine-learning risk prediction for rare outcomes has been pursued in the same clinical spirit [16]. High-dimensional inference for case probabilities is available under sparsity [17]; confidence-sequence theory supplies genuinely time-uniform uncertainty for unrestricted monitoring [18, 19], whereas the implementable construction developed here uses a prespecified finite monitoring grid; and case-control and surrogate-guided sampling use genuine observations more efficiently under severe imbalance [20, 21].

However, these ingredients have rarely been brought together. We do not propose another imbalance correction; rather, we are unaware of a single fixed-precision formulation that lets rare-event information, regularized risk estimation, a clinically meaningful threshold, and simultaneous uncertainty over planned monitoring looks jointly decide when accrual is sufficient. The clinically relevant target is a threshold decision over a patient population—not the precision of the coefficient vector, nor of a single predicted probability at one covariate value.

To supply that formulation, we build on the sequential fixed-accuracy program for logistic and generalized linear models—fixed-width sequential estimation [2, 3, 1], stopping-time asymptotics from nonlinear renewal theory [8, 7, 4], and β\beta-protected sequential estimation [5]—and repurpose it for a different object: sequential certification of a clinical threshold decision under event rarity. We first show why a natural whole-population stopping rule can be diluted by the overwhelming low-risk majority. Our primary proposal is therefore the decision-targeted rule T†T^{\dagger}, which controls both ambiguity and predictive width within the referral-relevant population. A simultaneous band over a prespecified finite monitoring schedule ensures that every decision certified at the selected monitored look is model-conditionally correct on the common coverage event. We then derive an oracle information benchmark that combines event rarity, profile-specific variance, and distance to the threshold, separating a model that is merely estimable from one whose decisions are certifiable. The classical stopping-time asymptotics and β\beta-protection that we draw on are not new; the contribution is the decision-targeted certification formulation and its rare-event interpretation. A genuinely time-uniform confidence sequence would extend the method to dense or unbounded monitoring, but that extension is not claimed for the finite-grid procedure studied here.

The remainder of the main paper follows the decision problem from method to evidence. Section 2 defines the rare-event model, simultaneous finite-grid band, and decision-targeted stopping rule, and states the central validity and first-order scaling results. Section 3 evaluates the rule in simulation, Section 4 gives the temporally validated NCHS application, and Section 5 discusses interpretation and scope. Appendices A–E contain the second-order stopping-time theory, complete proofs, additional estimator and sensitivity results, and the MODY-calibrated plasmode study.

2 Methodology

2.1 Model, decision, and predictive band

We first fix the four ingredients the rest of the section builds on: a rare-event logistic model, a single default estimator, the clinical decision the model serves, and the predictive band from which certification is read.

Separate the asymptotic rarity index from the sequential accrual index. Let r=1,2,…r=1,2,\ldots index a sequence of increasingly rare data-generating regimes and let ii index observations within a regime. We assume

Yr​i∣Xr​i=xr​i∼Bernoulli{pr(xr​i)},pr(x)=expit{γr+x⊤β0},γr→−∞.Y_{ri}\mid X_{ri}=x_{ri}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}\{p_{r}(x_{ri})\},\qquad p_{r}(x)=\expit\{\gamma_{r}+x^{\top}\beta_{0}\},\qquad\gamma_{r}\rightarrow-\infty. (1)

Writing ρr=eγr→0\rho_{r}=e^{\gamma_{r}}\rightarrow 0,

pr​(x)=ρr​ex⊤​β01+ρr​ex⊤​β0∼ρr​ex⊤​β0p_{r}(x)=\frac{\rho_{r}e^{x^{\top}\beta_{0}}}{1+\rho_{r}e^{x^{\top}\beta_{0}}}\sim\rho_{r}e^{x^{\top}\beta_{0}}

for fixed xx. For any given sequential experiment, the regime rr, its intercept γr\gamma_{r}, and hence its event distribution are fixed while the accrued sample size nn increases. This separation prevents the true event probability from appearing to change during monitoring. We suppress the index rr in fitted quantities when no ambiguity is possible.

Let θr=(γr,β0⊤)⊤\theta_{r}=(\gamma_{r},\beta_{0}^{\top})^{\top} and x~=(1,x⊤)⊤\widetilde{x}=(1,x^{\top})^{\top}. Our default implementation is ridge logistic regression with an unpenalized intercept,

θ^r,n=arg​maxθ⁡{ℓr,n​(θ)−12​θ⊤​Λn​θ},Λn=diag⁡(0,λn​Ip).\widehat{\theta}_{r,n}=\argmax_{\theta}\left\{\ell_{r,n}(\theta)-\tfrac{1}{2}\theta^{\top}\Lambda_{n}\theta\right\},\qquad\Lambda_{n}=\operatorname{diag}(0,\lambda_{n}I_{p}). (2)

It yields η^r,n​(x)=x~⊤​θ^r,n\widehat{\eta}_{r,n}(x)=\widetilde{x}^{\top}\widehat{\theta}_{r,n} and p^r,n​(x)=expit⁡{η^r,n​(x)}\widehat{p}_{r,n}(x)=\expit\{\widehat{\eta}_{r,n}(x)\}. Ridge is used as a stable default, not as an estimator for which validity is automatic. The certification argument below applies to any estimator satisfying the stated prediction-scale expansion and variance-consistency conditions. For ridge, a sufficient small-penalty condition for first-order centering is λn=o​{n​ρr}\lambda_{n}=o\{\sqrt{n\rho_{r}}\}; otherwise its prediction bias must be estimated and removed or incorporated into the band.

The action the model supports is a threshold decision. For a prespecified clinical threshold τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1), write c=logit⁡(τ)c=\logit(\tau); in regime rr, the target decision is

δr(x)=I{pr(x)≥τ}=I{ηr(x)≥c},ηr(x)=γr+x⊤β0.\delta_{r}(x)=I\{p_{r}(x)\geq\tau\}=I\{\eta_{r}(x)\geq c\},\qquad\eta_{r}(x)=\gamma_{r}+x^{\top}\beta_{0}. (3)

The threshold reflects clinical utility, treatment burden, or the relative costs of false positives and negatives, and for a rare outcome a fixed value of 0.50.5 is rarely appropriate.

Both the precision of p^n\widehat{p}_{n} and the certainty of this decision are read from a single object, a simultaneous predictive band over a prespecified finite monitoring schedule. Let [Lnη​(x),Unη​(x)][L_{n}^{\eta}(x),U_{n}^{\eta}(x)] cover the linear predictor simultaneously over the monitored sample sizes and a target set 𝒳0\mathcal{X}_{0},

Pr{ηr(x)∈[Lnη(x),Unη(x)] for every monitored n and every x∈𝒳0}≥1−α,\Prb_{r}\left\{\eta_{r}(x)\in[L_{n}^{\eta}(x),U_{n}^{\eta}(x)]\text{ for every monitored }n\text{ and every }x\in\mathcal{X}_{0}\right\}\geq 1-\alpha, (4)

with risk interval Lnp​(x)=expit⁡{Lnη​(x)}L_{n}^{p}(x)=\expit\{L_{n}^{\eta}(x)\}, Unp​(x)=expit⁡{Unη​(x)}U_{n}^{p}(x)=\expit\{U_{n}^{\eta}(x)\}. The same band serves both purposes: its width measures predictive precision, while its position relative to cc determines whether a classification is certified. A concrete construction is given next; for now it suffices that such a band exists.

Remark 1 (Alternative penalties).

Firth, Firth–ridge, elastic net, and Bayesian shrinkage are important comparators, but we do not treat each as a separate methodological branch; their role here is sensitivity analysis and supplementary comparison. Firth-type methods are particularly useful when separation is the dominant concern [11, 12, 13], though such penalization carries its own caveats for rare-disease regression [14].

2.2 Constructing the band

We make the band explicit rather than merely assume it. Fix a prespecified monitoring schedule 𝒩={n1<⋯<nK}\mathcal{N}=\{n_{1}<\cdots<n_{K}\} (a geometric grid in the experiments) and a finite target set 𝒳0\mathcal{X}_{0}.

Assumption 1 (Prediction-scale estimator regularity).

Consider a sequence of designs indexed by the rare-event regime rr, with finite monitoring schedules 𝒩r\mathcal{N}_{r} and finite target sets 𝒳0,r\mathcal{X}_{0,r}; subscripts are suppressed when no ambiguity is possible, and their cardinalities are fixed in the asymptotic argument. Let η^r,nbc​(x)\widehat{\eta}^{\mathrm{bc}}_{r,n}(x) denote the fitted linear predictor after any required first-order penalty-bias correction, and let V^r,n​(x)\widehat{V}_{r,n}(x) consistently estimate its variance. Uniformly over the finite set 𝒩r×𝒳0,r\mathcal{N}_{r}\times\mathcal{X}_{0,r}, as the smallest effective information minn∈𝒩r⁡n​ρr\min_{n\in\mathcal{N}_{r}}n\rho_{r} diverges,

η^r,nbc​(x)−ηr​(x)V^r,n​(x)→𝑑N⁡(0,1).\frac{\widehat{\eta}^{\mathrm{bc}}_{r,n}(x)-\eta_{r}(x)}{\sqrt{\widehat{V}_{r,n}(x)}}\ \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,1). (5)

For the ridge estimator in (2), one may take η^r,nbc=η^r,n\widehat{\eta}^{\mathrm{bc}}_{r,n}=\widehat{\eta}_{r,n} when λn=o​{n​ρr}\lambda_{n}=o\{\sqrt{n\rho_{r}}\}. A corresponding penalized model-based covariance is

Σ^r,n=(H^r,n+Λn)−1​H^r,n​(H^r,n+Λn)−1,V^r,n​(x)=x~⊤​Σ^r,n​x~,\widehat{\Sigma}_{r,n}=(\widehat{H}_{r,n}+\Lambda_{n})^{-1}\widehat{H}_{r,n}(\widehat{H}_{r,n}+\Lambda_{n})^{-1},\qquad\widehat{V}_{r,n}(x)=\widetilde{x}^{\top}\widehat{\Sigma}_{r,n}\widetilde{x}, (6)

where H^r,n\widehat{H}_{r,n} is the unpenalized observed information. If the penalty bias is not negligible, the centering must instead use a justified bias correction and its associated variance estimate.

Under Assumption 1, take

[Lnη​(x),Unη​(x)]=η^r,nbc​(x)±aα​V^r,n​(x),aα=Φ−1​(1−α2​K​|𝒳0|).[L_{n}^{\eta}(x),U_{n}^{\eta}(x)]=\widehat{\eta}^{\mathrm{bc}}_{r,n}(x)\pm a_{\alpha}\sqrt{\widehat{V}_{r,n}(x)},\qquad a_{\alpha}=\Phi^{-1}\!\Bigl(1-\tfrac{\alpha}{2K\,|\mathcal{X}_{0}|}\Bigr). (7)

A union bound over the K​|𝒳0|K\,|\mathcal{X}_{0}| monitored pairs then gives simultaneous coverage

Pr{ηr(x)∈[Lnη(x),Unη(x)]∀(n,x)∈𝒩×𝒳0}≥ 1−α\Prb_{r}\bigl\{\eta_{r}(x)\in[L_{n}^{\eta}(x),U_{n}^{\eta}(x)]\ \forall(n,x)\in\mathcal{N}\times\mathcal{X}_{0}\bigr\}\ \geq\ 1-\alpha

(asymptotically, from the per-look normal approximation). For a fixed finite collection of monitored pairs, each marginal noncoverage probability is at most α/(K​|𝒳0|)+o⁡(1)\alpha/(K|\mathcal{X}_{0}|)+o(1), so Bonferroni gives total noncoverage at most α+o⁡(1)\alpha+o(1). A growing collection would require additional control of the sum of the approximation errors; pointwise normality alone does not supply that control.

Remark 2 (Finite-grid simultaneous validity).

This is the band used in Study 4 (Section 3.1), where the naive fixed-nn choice aα=z1−α/2a_{\alpha}=z_{1-\alpha/2} is shown to violate the guarantee under repeated looks while the corrected aαa_{\alpha} restores it. The union bound is deliberately simple and pays a log⁡(K​|𝒳0|)\log(K|\mathcal{X}_{0}|) width penalty; for dense or unbounded monitoring a genuine time-uniform confidence sequence [18] can replace it. The present construction is not claimed to be valid outside the prespecified finite schedule 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Remark 3 (Scope of certification).

The guarantee below is model-conditional: it certifies the threshold decision defined by the working logistic risk pr​(x)p_{r}(x), provided Assumption 1 and the simultaneous coverage statement hold. Under link or linear-predictor misspecification, coverage of the working-model target does not by itself certify the true clinical risk. Out-of-sample calibration and decision performance are therefore separate empirical requirements, not consequences of the certification theorem.

Define the certified set

𝒞n={x∈𝒳0:Unη​(x)<c​or​Lnη​(x)>c},𝒰n=𝒳0∖𝒞n.\mathcal{C}_{n}=\left\{x\in\mathcal{X}_{0}:\ U_{n}^{\eta}(x)<c\ \text{or}\ L_{n}^{\eta}(x)>c\right\},\qquad\mathcal{U}_{n}=\mathcal{X}_{0}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{n}.

If QQ denotes the target covariate distribution, define the ambiguity mass An=Q⁡(𝒰n)A_{n}=Q(\mathcal{U}_{n}) and the predictive width functional

Pn=Q1−γ​[Unp​(X)−Lnp​(X)].P_{n}=Q_{1-\gamma}\left[U_{n}^{p}(X)-L_{n}^{p}(X)\right].

Both are computed from the same finite-grid simultaneous band.

2.3 Whole-population baseline and decision-targeted certification

A natural baseline controls ambiguity and width over the entire target population:

Ψnall=max{Anε,Pnd},Tall=inf{n∈𝒩:n≥nmin,Ψnall≤1}.\Psi_{n}^{\mathrm{all}}=\max\left\{\frac{A_{n}}{\varepsilon},\frac{P_{n}}{d}\right\},\qquad T^{\mathrm{all}}=\inf\left\{n\in\mathcal{N}:\ n\geq n_{\min},\;\Psi_{n}^{\mathrm{all}}\leq 1\right\}. (8)

Thus TallT^{\mathrm{all}} stops when no more than an ε\varepsilon fraction of the entire target population is classification-ambiguous and the (1−γ)(1-\gamma)-quantile of its risk-interval width is at most dd. We use this rule as a comparator, not as the primary proposal.

The functional Ψnall\Psi_{n}^{\mathrm{all}} measures ambiguity as a fraction of the entire target population. Under extreme rarity this is too weak: as information accrues, the overwhelming low-risk majority becomes certified below the threshold, so An=Q⁡(𝒰n)A_{n}=Q(\mathcal{U}_{n}) can be small and the risk interval can be narrow where pr​(x)≈0p_{r}(x)\approx 0 long before the few referral-relevant patients are resolved. The baseline may then fire with very few genuine events, certifying little more than refer essentially no one.

Our primary rule prevents this dilution by targeting the decision-relevant population. Split the certified set into its two decisions,

𝒞n+={x:Lnη​(x)>c}​(certify refer),𝒞n−={x:Unη​(x)<c}​(certify do-not-refer),\mathcal{C}_{n}^{+}=\{x:L_{n}^{\eta}(x)>c\}\ (\text{certify refer}),\qquad\mathcal{C}_{n}^{-}=\{x:U_{n}^{\eta}(x)<c\}\ (\text{certify do-not-refer}),

leaving 𝒰n\mathcal{U}_{n} ambiguous, and let the referral-relevant region be the profiles not already certified below the threshold,

ℛn=𝒰n∪𝒞n+={x:Unη​(x)≥c}.\mathcal{R}_{n}=\mathcal{U}_{n}\cup\mathcal{C}_{n}^{+}=\{x:U_{n}^{\eta}(x)\geq c\}.

Define the decision-targeted ambiguity and width

An†=Q⁡(𝒰n)Q⁡(ℛn),Pn†=Q1−γ​[Unp​(X)−Lnp​(X)|X∈ℛn],A_{n}^{\dagger}=\frac{Q(\mathcal{U}_{n})}{Q(\mathcal{R}_{n})},\qquad P_{n}^{\dagger}=Q_{1-\gamma}\!\left[\,U_{n}^{p}(X)-L_{n}^{p}(X)\ \middle|\ X\in\mathcal{R}_{n}\right], (9)

when Q⁡(ℛn)>0Q(\mathcal{R}_{n})>0. If Q⁡(ℛn)=0Q(\mathcal{R}_{n})=0, set An†=Pn†=0A_{n}^{\dagger}=P_{n}^{\dagger}=0. In this empty-set case every target profile has already been certified below the referral threshold, so no referral-relevant width remains to be controlled. The proposed decision-targeted rule is

Ψn†=max{An†ε,Pn†d},T†=inf{n∈𝒩:n≥nmin,Ψn†≤1}.\Psi_{n}^{\dagger}=\max\left\{\frac{A_{n}^{\dagger}}{\varepsilon},\frac{P_{n}^{\dagger}}{d}\right\},\qquad T^{\dagger}=\inf\left\{n\in\mathcal{N}:\ n\geq n_{\min},\;\Psi_{n}^{\dagger}\leq 1\right\}. (10)

Now An†A_{n}^{\dagger} is the ambiguous fraction among patients who might be referred, and Pn†P_{n}^{\dagger} controls precision only where a decision is at stake. When the threshold lies in the bulk of QQ (so ℛn=𝒳0\mathcal{R}_{n}=\mathcal{X}_{0}) the two rules coincide; the refinement matters precisely when the action concerns a rare region.

Proposition 1 (Relation between the baseline and decision-targeted rules).

At a monitored look with Q⁡(ℛn)>0Q(\mathcal{R}_{n})>0, An†=An/Q⁡(ℛn)≥AnA_{n}^{\dagger}=A_{n}/Q(\mathcal{R}_{n})\geq A_{n}. If ℛn=𝒳0\mathcal{R}_{n}=\mathcal{X}_{0} at every eligible look, then Ψn†=Ψnall\Psi_{n}^{\dagger}=\Psi_{n}^{\mathrm{all}} and T†=TallT^{\dagger}=T^{\mathrm{all}}. More generally, there is no unconditional ordering of the stopping times because Pn†P_{n}^{\dagger} is a conditional quantile and the empty-relevant-set convention can make it zero. If Pn†≥PnP_{n}^{\dagger}\geq P_{n} at every eligible look, however, then Ψn†≥Ψnall\Psi_{n}^{\dagger}\geq\Psi_{n}^{\mathrm{all}} and T†≥TallT^{\dagger}\geq T^{\mathrm{all}}. In particular, if the baseline stops at a look for which An†>εA_{n}^{\dagger}>\varepsilon or Pn†>dP_{n}^{\dagger}>d, that stop is premature for the decision-targeted criterion.

Proof.

The ambiguity inequality follows from 0<Q⁡(ℛn)≤10<Q(\mathcal{R}_{n})\leq 1. When ℛn=𝒳0\mathcal{R}_{n}=\mathcal{X}_{0}, the ambiguity masses and width quantiles coincide. Under the additional width ordering, both components of the maximum defining Ψn†\Psi_{n}^{\dagger} are at least their whole-population counterparts, which gives the stopping-time ordering. The final statement follows directly from the definition of T†T^{\dagger}. ∎

Proposition 2 (Validity is inherited).

Under the coverage hypothesis of Theorem 1, every decision certified at the prespecified-grid-selected time T†T^{\dagger} of (10), whenever that time is finite, is model-conditionally correct simultaneously with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha.

Argument (from Theorem 1, no new proof needed). Theorem 1 guarantees that, on the simultaneous-coverage event, every profile placed in 𝒞n+∪𝒞n−\mathcal{C}_{n}^{+}\cup\mathcal{C}_{n}^{-} at every prespecified monitored time carries the correct decision. The decision-targeted rule changes only the stopping criterion, not the per-profile certified set; since T†∈𝒩T^{\dagger}\in\mathcal{N} whenever it is finite, the one simultaneous coverage event validates all decisions certified at that time. No decision is certified by a rule that has not stopped. □\square

Remark 4 (Synthetic oversampling is not a source of information).

We do not devote a section to synthetic oversampling such as SMOTE; one statistical observation suffices. If synthetic data SS are generated conditionally from the observed data DD by a mechanism q⁡(s∣d)q(s\mid d) that does not depend on the unknown parameter, then fθ​(d,s)=fθ​(d)​q​(s∣d)f_{\theta}(d,s)=f_{\theta}(d)\,q(s\mid d), so the joint score equals the score from DD alone. Synthetic rows may change an optimization objective, but they do not create new independent likelihood information. The proposed decision-targeted stopping rule therefore counts only genuine accrued information.

Remark 5 (Why the refinement is not vacuous).

Under the whole-population baseline, An≤εA_{n}\leq\varepsilon can hold while ℛn\mathcal{R}_{n} remains mostly ambiguous. Normalising by Q⁡(ℛn)Q(\mathcal{R}_{n}) removes this dilution. Theorem 2 supplies an oracle information benchmark for resolving an individual margin; it does not imply a rate for T†T^{\dagger}. The population rule must also meet its conditional width requirement, which can remain binding even after individual decisions are resolved.

Note that for positive sequences ara_{r} and brb_{r}, the notation ar≍bra_{r}\asymp b_{r} means that they have the same order in the asymptotic regime under discussion: there exist constants 0<c≤C<∞0<c\leq C<\infty, independent of rr, such that c​br≤ar≤C​brc\,b_{r}\leq a_{r}\leq C\,b_{r} for all sufficiently large rr. It does not mean that ar/br→1a_{r}/b_{r}\to 1; ratio convergence to one is denoted by ar∼bra_{r}\sim b_{r}. When the index is nn, the same convention is used with “sufficiently large nn.”

2.4 Theoretical properties

We establish rare-event information scaling, simultaneous-grid model-conditional validity, and an oracle first-passage result with explicit conditions for transfer to pointwise certification. Complete proofs are provided in Appendix B, and the classical second-order stopping-time development is provided in Appendix A.

2.4.1 Rare-event information scaling

Let X~=(1,X⊤)⊤\widetilde{X}=(1,X^{\top})^{\top}. In regime rr, the information after nn observations is 𝑰r,n=∑i=1npr​(Xr​i)​{1−pr​(Xr​i)}​X~r​i​X~r​i⊤.\bm{I}_{r,n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_{r}(X_{ri})\{1-p_{r}(X_{ri})\}\widetilde{X}_{ri}\widetilde{X}_{ri}^{\top}.

Assumption 2 (Rare-event moments).

The Xr​iX_{ri} are i.i.d. within each regime, E⁡[eX⊤​β0​‖X~‖2]<∞\E[e^{X^{\top}\beta_{0}}\|\widetilde{X}\|^{2}]<\infty, and 𝑱=E⁡[eX⊤​β0​X~​X~⊤]\bm{J}=\E\left[e^{X^{\top}\beta_{0}}\widetilde{X}\widetilde{X}^{\top}\right] is positive definite on the effective model subspace.

Proposition 3 (Effective rare-event information).

Under Assumption 2 and a triangular-array law of large numbers,

𝑰r,nn​ρr​⟶𝑝​𝑱as ​r,n→∞​ with ​n​ρr→∞.\frac{\bm{I}_{r,n}}{n\rho_{r}}\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\bm{J}\qquad\text{as }r,n\to\infty\text{ with }n\rho_{r}\to\infty.

The interpretation is effective information size≍n​ρr.\text{effective information size}\asymp n\rho_{r}.

2.4.2 Validity of certified classifications at the stopping time and pointwise certification complexity

The theorem below is about decision certification, not convergence of a monitored trajectory.

Theorem 1 (Simultaneous-grid model-conditional decision certification).

Suppose the band [Lnη​(x),Unη​(x)][L_{n}^{\eta}(x),U_{n}^{\eta}(x)] has simultaneous coverage over every (n,x)∈𝒩×𝒳0(n,x)\in\mathcal{N}\times\mathcal{X}_{0} with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha. Let SS be any data-dependent monitored look taking values in 𝒩∪{∞}\mathcal{N}\cup\{\infty\}, including TallT^{\mathrm{all}} or T†T^{\dagger}, where infinity denotes no stop. Then, with probability at least 1−α1-\alpha, whenever S<∞S<\infty, every decision certified at SS is model-conditionally correct:

For a target profile xrx_{r} in regime rr, write mr=|ηr​(xr)−cr|>0m_{r}=|\eta_{r}(x_{r})-c_{r}|>0, where crc_{r} is the prespecified log-odds threshold; a fixed profile or threshold is included when appropriate. Define

Remark 6 (Interpretation and scope of the rate).

Theorem 2 separates three requirements: enough effective information before monitoring, exclusion of premature crossings, and a monitoring grid that becomes dense on the n⋆,rn_{\star,r} scale. The normal approximation in Assumption 1 alone does not imply (13): near n⋆,rn_{\star,r}, the standard error divided by mrm_{r} is approximately 1/aα,r1/a_{\alpha,r}, which need not vanish for a fixed critical value. Neither ratio limit is asserted for the fixed geometric grids used in our numerical studies. On a geometric grid with a fixed spacing ratio, rounding alone can prevent ratio convergence to one.

The deterministic benchmark n⋆,rn_{\star,r} exposes the joint effects of rarity, margin, and profile-specific variance. When aα,r2​vra_{\alpha,r}^{2}v_{r} is bounded above and away from zero, it has order 1/(ρr​mr2)1/(\rho_{r}m_{r}^{2}); this is an oracle information scale, not a proved rate for the population stopping rule T†T^{\dagger}, whose width criterion can also be binding. The assumptions require a compatible joint limit. In particular, with fixed xx, fixed τ\tau, and bounded aα,r2​vra_{\alpha,r}^{2}v_{r}, letting ρr→0\rho_{r}\to 0 makes mrm_{r} grow and n⋆,r​ρr→0n_{\star,r}\rho_{r}\to 0; that regime is excluded. A vanishing-margin regime with sufficiently large nmin,r​ρrn_{\min,r}\rho_{r}, for example, can satisfy the oracle conditions. Appendix A instead uses a fixed-regime precision limit.

Under separate bounded-information assumptions, Appendix A develops an oracle normal approximation, expected stopping-time correction, and β\beta-protected design quantile. Those oracle calculations clarify the fluctuation scale but are not used as validity evidence for the implementable finite-grid rule evaluated below.

3 Simulation evaluation

3.1 Simulation design and operating characteristics

The revised simulation study evaluates the procedure actually defined in Sections 2.2–2.3. We generate X∼N5​(0,Σ)X\sim N_{5}(0,\Sigma), with Σj​k=0.3|j−k|\Sigma_{jk}=0.3^{|j-k|}, and use β=(0.8,−0.6,0.5,−0.4,0.3)⊤\beta=(0.8,-0.6,0.5,-0.4,0.3)^{\top}. Unless otherwise stated, Y|XY\mid X follows the correctly specified logistic model, the intercept is calibrated to the stated marginal prevalence π\pi, and the decision threshold is τ=0.10\tau=0.10. We take (ε,d,γ)=(0.10,0.10,0.10)(\varepsilon,d,\gamma)=(0.10,0.10,0.10). At every scheduled look the ridge fit uses an unpenalised intercept, λ=1\lambda=1, and the penalised sandwich covariance in Assumption 1.

For the rule-comparison study the target set contains M=60M=60 distinct profiles and the schedule contains K=14K=14 looks. Consequently every sequential band uses

aα=Φ−1​{1−0.052​K​M}=4.015,a_{\alpha}=\Phi^{-1}\!\left\{1-\frac{0.05}{2KM}\right\}=4.015,

not the repeatedly read fixed-sample value 1.96. The target distribution is constructed so that a fraction q∈{0.02,0.10}q\in\{0.02,0.10\} lies above the referral threshold at log-odds margin m∈{0.30,0.75}m\in\{0.30,0.75\}, while the remainder is well below it. The same stream is used for all stopping rules within a replication. There are 1,000 replications in every rule-comparison, monitoring, estimator, and robustness cell. We report restricted medians and interquartile ranges for censored stopping times, censoring percentages, event-count means with Monte Carlo standard errors, and Wilson 95% intervals for coverage and error probabilities. The submission Data Files contain the frozen numerical summaries used for these tables and figures together with a clean reference implementation of the documented Study 1–4 certification mechanics and configurations. The final historical replication-level files and exact seeds were not retained, so byte-for-byte regeneration of those particular Monte Carlo summaries is not claimed; where a historical nuisance tuning value was not recorded, the reference implementation exposes it explicitly rather than imputing provenance.

3.2 Study 1: when does decision targeting matter?

Table 1 gives the direct comparison that motivates the primary rule. The whole-population baseline can stop after the low-risk majority becomes easy to classify: its median ranges from only 500 to 13,585 patients. In contrast, T†T^{\dagger} waits for uncertainty among patients who might actually be referred. At π=0.02\pi=0.02, its restricted median is 42,268–65,874; at π=0.005\pi=0.005, it reaches the 640,000-patient horizon in most scenarios. In the two most difficult near-threshold settings, 17.5% and 29.5% of replications remain uncertified at that horizon. Thus the low-risk majority can make TallT^{\mathrm{all}} smaller by one to two orders of magnitude without resolving the clinically actionable part of the target population.

The Wilson lower limits for simultaneous coverage range from 97.7% to 99.1%, consistent with the nominal guarantee and the conservatism expected from a Bonferroni band over correlated profiles. A coefficient-stability comparator and a fixed-30-event comparator stop much earlier. The fixed-event rule never satisfies the decision-targeted criterion, while the coefficient-stability rule does so in only 0.5% of one scenario and never in the other seven (8000 paired replications total). Figure 1 displays the separation between the two population rules.

3.3 Study 2: estimable does not mean certifiable

We next compare MLE, ridge, Firth, and FLIC on the same rare-event streams (π=0.02\pi=0.02). All four algorithms return finite converged fits in this low-dimensional experiment. Their coefficient norms are already similar after only about ten events, and nearly indistinguishable by n=8000n=8000; nevertheless, none of the 1,000 replications is decision-certified at n≤8000n\leq 8000. At n=64,000n=64{,}000, with about 1283 genuine events, the four estimators certify in 99.3–99.4% of replications. Thus the finding is not an artefact of one penalisation method: successful and stable-looking estimation occurs far earlier than simultaneous decision certification.

The full estimator-by-look comparison, including Monte Carlo uncertainty, is reported in Appendix C, Table C1.

3.4 Study 3: model-conditional coverage is not clinical truth

The certification theorem is conditional on the working logistic model. To make that limitation empirical, Table 2 compares correct specification, an omitted centred quadratic term, a probit data-generating link, and a shifted target covariate distribution. “Working coverage” refers to the pseudo-true logistic linear predictor, whereas false decisions are evaluated against the actual data-generating risk.

Under correct specification, working coverage is 99.2% and no false clinical decision occurs. Under the omitted quadratic, working coverage falls to 93.5% and every stopped replication contains at least one falsely certified target profile, even though the mean false-decision fraction is only 1.67% (one of 60 profiles). The probit link is benign in this design, while covariate shift preserves decision correctness but increases the median T†T^{\dagger} from 34,333 to 98,841. These results support the precise claim made by the theory: the band certifies a working-model target, and empirical calibration and specification checks remain necessary for clinical interpretation.

3.5 Study 4: is repeated-monitoring adjustment necessary?

We construct 40 distinct profiles exactly on the decision boundary and evaluate the family-wise probability that at least one interval excludes that boundary over the complete look-by-profile grid. This is a simultaneous-coverage failure and would produce an unjustified certification away from the boundary. It is not automatically a wrong binary classification because the convention in (3) assigns equality to the positive class. At one final look, ordinary pointwise 1.96 intervals already have an 18.9% family-wise boundary-exclusion probability because 40 profiles are inspected. Re-reading them at 20 planned looks raises this probability to 76.2%. In contrast, the finite-grid band remains between 0.4% and 0.5%; its upper Wilson limit never exceeds 1.2%. The conservatism reflects strong dependence among the nested looks and target profiles, but the required simultaneous-coverage inequality is maintained.

Earlier fixed-1.96 scaling plots are not used as evidence for sequential validity. The documented oracle precision experiment in Appendix C examines the stopping-time approximations only; it is not validity evidence for the implementable finite-grid procedure.

4 NCHS linked birth/infant-death application

The observed-data analysis asks whether the whole-population and decision-targeted rules reach the same conclusion when infant-mortality records accrue, and whether apparently stable external prediction performance is sufficient for decision certification. Development uses 2013 records, while a disjoint 2014 sample supplies temporal outcome validation.

4.1 Data, target population, and monitoring design

We used the official 2013 and 2014 US Cohort Linked Birth/Infant Death public-use denominator files [22, 23]; the endpoint is linked death within the first year of life. We retained residence codes 1–3 and excluded code 4 (foreign residents). A full fixed-width scan then gave 3,932,1813{,}932{,}181 resident births and 23,14223{,}142 linked deaths in 2013 (0.5885%0.5885\%), and 3,988,0763{,}988{,}076 and 23,25623{,}256, respectively, in 2014 (0.5831%0.5831\%). These counts refer to the complete resident cohorts, not to the sampled development and validation records.

The sequential development sample was a reproducible reservoir sample of 300,000300{,}000 2013 resident births, containing 1,6601{,}660 deaths. The ridge logistic model used twelve variables available at birth: birth weight, gestational age, plurality, maternal-age group, infant sex, prenatal-care month and prenatal-visit recode, maternal smoking, maternal education, and indicators for Black, Hispanic, and other race/ethnicity. The prenatal-visit variable is the ordinal PREVIS_REC category (01–11), not the raw visit count; code 12 denotes missingness. Unknown race/ethnicity makes all three indicators missing before imputation, rather than assigning the reference category. Official reporting flags and year-specific race/ethnicity codes were handled by the same audited decoder in preparation and analysis. Medians, centring, and scaling were estimated once from the complete 300,000-record development sample’s covariates and then frozen; the ridge penalty was λ=1\lambda=1, with an unpenalised intercept and the penalised sandwich covariance specified above.

The target distribution QQ was the empirical distribution of a fixed 4,0004{,}000-profile sample from the 2014 cohort. A disjoint 2014 sample of 100,000100{,}000 births with 561561 deaths was reserved for temporal outcome validation. Target outcomes were not used in fitting or stopping and were read only for post-stopping description. Because the public-use files suppress exact birth date, the twelve birth months were kept in chronological order and records were randomised only within month. We generated 1,0001{,}000 pseudo-streams. Thus replication uncertainty describes unknown within-month ordering, not independent population-sampling uncertainty. This is a retrospective experiment using completed infant-death follow-up and a fixed future-year covariate target, not a simulation of when outcomes would become observable in real time. Prospective deployment would require an outcome-availability schedule and an independently fixed or predictably updated preprocessing and target-population specification.

We fitted the model at 18 prespecified looks from 500 through 300,000300{,}000 births. To exclude the extremely sparse startup regime from certification, the minimum eligible size was nmin=14,783n_{\min}=14{,}783, the first scheduled look with at least 80 expected deaths under the audited 2013 event rate. Earlier fits were retained only as accrual diagnostics. There were 54 nonconverged fits at 500 births and 13 at 728 births; these were omitted from diagnostic summaries. Every fit at 1,061 births and thereafter converged, including all eligible looks. The two-sided normal band was nevertheless Bonferroni-adjusted over all 18×4,000=72,00018\times 4{,}000=72{,}000 fitted look–profile pairs (α=0.05\alpha=0.05, critical value 4.9634.963), making it conservative for the eligible subset. The eligibility restriction is enforced for both rules in all 27 settings. All reported NCHS results were regenerated with this restriction and the common decoder; no stopping-time row from an earlier implementation is reused.

The width functional was the 90th percentile (γ=0.10\gamma=0.10). Under the primary specification (τ,d,ε)=(0.05,0.01,0.10)(\tau,d,\varepsilon)=(0.05,0.01,0.10), τ=0.05\tau=0.05 is an illustrative elevated-risk follow-up threshold rather than an established clinical policy; d=0.01d=0.01 requires an absolute-risk interval width no greater than one percentage point for at least 90% of referral-relevant profiles; and ε=0.10\varepsilon=0.10 requires at least 90% of that region to have a resolved threshold decision. These quantities should be elicited with clinicians and fixed before monitoring in a prospective application. Sensitivity analyses crossed τ∈{0.01,0.025,0.05}\tau\in\{0.01,0.025,0.05\}, d∈{0.01,0.025,0.05}d\in\{0.01,0.025,0.05\}, and ε∈{0.05,0.10,0.20}\varepsilon\in\{0.05,0.10,0.20\}.

4.2 Stopping behavior and sensitivity

The paired comparison exposes the imbalance problem directly (Table 4 and Figure 4). Under the primary specification, TallT^{\mathrm{all}} certified in all 1,000 pseudo-streams at the 141,345-birth look, after a mean 808.2 genuine deaths. Its whole-population ambiguity and width met their tolerances (Aall=0.0134A_{\mathrm{all}}=0.0134, Pall=0.00840P_{\mathrm{all}}=0.00840), but among profiles that might be referred the ambiguity was A†=0.568A_{\dagger}=0.568 and the risk-band width was P†=0.289P_{\dagger}=0.289. The whole-population stop therefore left 56.8% of the referral-relevant region unresolved.

In contrast, T†T^{\dagger} did not certify in any primary pseudo-stream by the prespecified horizon H=300,000H=300{,}000; this is right censoring, not a stopping time of 300,000. At HH, after all 1,660 sampled deaths, referral-relevant ambiguity was still 0.4100.410, width was 0.2130.213, and Ψ†​(H)=21.27>1\Psi^{\dagger}(H)=21.27>1. No T†T^{\dagger} stop occurred in any of the 27 sensitivity cells; even the least restrictive cell had Ψ†​(H)=3.09\Psi^{\dagger}(H)=3.09. By comparison, TallT^{\mathrm{all}} stopped in 24 of the 27 cells.

These results illustrate how acceptable whole-population precision can coexist with substantial uncertainty among patients who might be referred. By evaluating ambiguity and interval width within this group, the proposed rule withheld certification while the referral-specific requirements remained unmet. In this retrospective analysis, its value is to prevent the low-risk majority from obscuring decision-relevant uncertainty; the results do not establish improved predictive accuracy or clinical benefit.

The complete 27-cell threshold–tolerance table and terminal-criterion heatmap are reported in Appendix D, Table D1 and Figure D1.

4.3 Temporal validation and limitations

Temporal validation gives a complementary result (Table 5 and Figure 5; threshold-specific results are in Appendix D, Table D2). At TallT^{\mathrm{all}}, the 2014 calibration intercept was −0.008-0.008, calibration slope 0.9650.965, Brier score 0.004270.00427, log loss 0.023150.02315, ROC-AUC 0.8520.852, and PR-AUC 0.3720.372. At τ=0.05\tau=0.05, sensitivity was 0.5010.501, specificity 0.9890.989, PPV 0.1970.197, NPV 0.9970.997, and net benefit 0.002210.00221, compared with zero for treat-none and −0.0467-0.0467 for treat-all. The horizon/full-development-sample fit produced very similar point-prediction metrics (ROC-AUC 0.8540.854, PR-AUC 0.3730.373). The juxtaposition is substantive: apparently stable external point-prediction performance does not imply that simultaneous uncertainty is narrow enough to certify referral-region decisions.

The application has five important limitations. First, pseudo-streams preserve birth month but cannot recover suppressed within-month chronology or actual outcome-availability times; completed outcomes and frozen full-sample covariate preprocessing make the analysis retrospective. Second, the stopping horizon is the sampled 300,000300{,}000 births, so the study provides only the lower bound T†>300,000T^{\dagger}>300{,}000 under the examined design. Third, linked public-use data may omit deaths that could not be linked to a birth record. Fourth, the threshold and predictor model are methodological examples, not a validated clinical referral policy. Fifth, the minimum eligible size removes the most severely data-sparse looks but does not turn the asymptotic normal band into an exact finite-sample procedure; estimator regularity and calibration must still be assessed in each application. These cautions prevent the non-stopping result from being overstated while preserving its central message: class-imbalance dilution can make whole-population certification materially misleading.

A MODY-calibrated plasmode stress test, retained explicitly as simulated rather than observed-data evidence, is reported in Appendix E.

5 Discussion

For a rare medical outcome the meaningful sample size is not the raw number of patients but the number of informative rare-event contributions, which under the rare-event logistic model appears through the effective scale n​ρrn\rho_{r}. The procedure proposed here uses that information to answer a practical clinical question—whether the predicted risks, and the decisions taken from them at a prespecified threshold, are already precise enough to act on—without creating synthetic events and without requiring precise estimation of every regression coefficient. It moves fixed-precision stopping from the coefficient vector to a decision-targeted certification over a clinical target population. The whole-population rule is a baseline; the primary rule T†T^{\dagger} controls ambiguity and width among patients who might be referred. A single simultaneous predictive band over prespecified monitoring looks supplies both estimation precision and model-conditional decision certification at the selected look. The present guarantee is finite-grid and is not an unrestricted anytime-validity claim. The absolute stopping times also depend on the chosen simultaneous-band construction. Bonferroni deliberately ignores dependence among nested looks and target profiles; a calibrated max-statistic or multiplier/bootstrap construction could reduce this conservatism while preserving the same prespecified-grid principle. Accordingly, the NCHS finding that T†>300,000T^{\dagger}>300{,}000 should be read as a conservative certification benchmark under the present band, not as an intrinsic minimum cohort size. In 1,000-replication experiments per cell, the whole-population baseline stops one to two orders of magnitude before T†T^{\dagger} in rare actionable regions, while coefficient stability or 30 accrued events almost never meet the decision-targeted criterion. The misspecification study further shows why working-model coverage must not be interpreted as calibration to the true clinical risk. The temporally validated NCHS analysis makes the same distinction in observed data: TallT^{\mathrm{all}} stopped at the 141,345-birth look while 56.8% of referral-relevant profiles remained ambiguous, whereas T†T^{\dagger} was right-censored at 300,000 births in every tolerance-grid cell. The 2014 point-prediction metrics were already close to their full-development-sample values, showing that stable discrimination and calibration summaries do not by themselves establish decision certifiability. The oracle information benchmark depends on rarity and the decision margin through n⋆,r=aα,r2​vr/(ρr​mr2)n_{\star,r}=a_{\alpha,r}^{2}v_{r}/(\rho_{r}m_{r}^{2}). Theorem 2 states the additional conditions needed for first-passage ratio limits; these are not asserted for the fixed-grid population rule. In practice, the simulations and the infant-mortality application illustrate that a regularized model can look estimable well before its absolute-risk decisions are certifiable. Regularization, separation diagnostics, and stability screening support this account rather than becoming parallel stories.

We have deliberately kept the scope narrow. Ridge is used for stability rather than as an optimal estimator; its inferential use requires the stated small-penalty condition or an explicit penalty-bias correction, and all certification claims remain conditional on the working risk model. Unrestricted p≫np\gg n estimation, the boundary degeneracy of near-zero or near-one probabilities and its reverse-martingale characterization, and cost-based optimal stopping are separate problems treated elsewhere or left for later. Natural extensions include more general joint rare-event, vanishing-margin, and growing-target-set asymptotics; high-dimensional certification under sparsity, adaptive or surrogate-guided acquisition of genuine events, and application to population-scale genomic and electronic-health-record cohorts once the corresponding controlled-access data can be used. A further direction is to replace absolute-risk thresholds by treatment-specific utilities or individualized causal contrasts; that extension would require causal identification, longitudinal updating, and adaptive-regime validation, so the present paper should be read as a prediction-to-decision certification framework rather than a full adaptive-treatment theory.

Appendices A–E provide the second-order oracle precision development and β\beta-protected design calculation, complete proofs, detailed estimator and NCHS sensitivity tables, and the MODY-calibrated plasmode. Placing these supporting results after the Discussion keeps the main text centered on the clinical decision problem, the implementable rule, and its observed-data evidence while retaining a single self-contained manuscript.

Remark A.1 (Stopping changes the second-order correction).

The term −ζ2/q2-\zeta^{2}/q^{2} is essential: substituting a fixed-sample expansion at a random stopping time would omit it. Because the weights here are oracle weights, this result does not establish a regret correction for fitted ridge or Firth estimators.

Definition A.1 (β\beta-protected oracle precision).

For fixed β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), an integer sample size nn is (h,β)(h,\beta)-protected at xx if P{aαVn≤h}≥1−β\Prb\{a_{\alpha}\sqrt{V_{n}}\leq h\}\geq 1-\beta.

The coverage level 1−α1-\alpha and planning level 1−β1-\beta have different roles: the former concerns a predictive band, whereas the latter budgets observations for the oracle precision target [5]. No second-order claim for T†T^{\dagger} follows from this appendix.

Appendix C Additional numerical results

C.1 Estimator sensitivity

Table C1 gives the detailed MLE, ridge, Firth, and FLIC comparison summarized in the main paper. All methods return finite fits well before their decisions become certifiable.

C.2 Oracle second-order diagnostic

We ran a separate, fully specified experiment for the oracle precision limit in Appendix A. Let X∼Uniform⁡[−1,1]X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[-1,1], p⁡(X)=expit⁡{log⁡(0.02/0.98)+0.8​X}p(X)=\expit\{\log(0.02/0.98)+0.8X\}, and z=(1,1)⊤z=(1,1)^{\top}. We used true information weights, aα=1.96a_{\alpha}=1.96, every integer look, and h=aα​q/n0h=a_{\alpha}\sqrt{q/n_{0}} for n0∈{375,750,1500,3000,6000}n_{0}\in\{375,750,1500,3000,6000\}. There were 1,000 independent streams, paired across the five settings, with no censoring; the seed was 20260828. Gauss–Legendre quadrature with 128 nodes, checked against 256 nodes, gave q=136.013q=136.013, κ2=1.888\kappa^{2}=1.888, and δ/q−ζ2/q2=0.348\delta/q-\zeta^{2}/q^{2}=0.348.

Table C2 reports stopping-time means, scaled variances, and protection quantiles. To examine the mean correction without the leading centered-sum fluctuation, Table C3 also reports Dh=Nh−n0−Oh+SNh/qD_{h}=N_{h}-n_{0}-O_{h}+S_{N_{h}}/q, using the notation of Appendix B.4. Since E⁡SNh=0\E S_{N_{h}}=0, E⁡Dh→δ/q−ζ2/q2\E D_{h}\to\delta/q-\zeta^{2}/q^{2}. The normal budgets achieved empirical precision probabilities from 94.1% to 95.5%; finite-sample and Monte Carlo discrepancies remain. Figure C1 displays the normal approximation and centered correction. This is a diagnostic of the stated oracle expansions, not a proof of them or evidence for sequential-band validity or exact finite-sample protection. Code, all 5,000 replication-setting rows, and generated tables and figures accompany the submission.

Appendix D Full NCHS sensitivity and threshold performance

Table D1 and Figure D1 report all 27 prespecified threshold–tolerance cells. The decision-targeted rule is right-censored in every cell. Table D2 gives the detailed 2014 threshold-performance comparison.

Appendix E MODY-calibrated plasmode stress test

This plasmode considers population-scale screening for maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY), motivated by an All of Us genotype-first study of N=374,973N=374{,}973 participants [24, 25]. No individual-level All of Us records enter the analysis. The simulation uses twelve standardized clinical predictors, full-model AUC approximately 0.91, a genetic-testing threshold τ=0.10\tau=0.10, and tolerances (d,ε)=(0.05,0.10)(d,\varepsilon)=(0.05,0.10). Two prevalences bracket the motivating settings: π=0.02\pi=0.02 among people with diabetes and π=0.003\pi=0.003 in a general genotype-first cohort. Results average 1,000 accrual orderings.

Among people with diabetes, the high-risk phenotype is certified after about 680 patients in every ordering, while the borderline profile is not certified in 53% of orderings. In the general cohort, positive referral for the high-risk profile is certifiable in only about half the orderings even at 400,000 participants, and the borderline profile is not certified in 43% of orderings. The study therefore supports enrichment before certification. It is a prevalence-and-enrichment stress test, not a second observed-data validation.

Reproducibility

All simulation and NCHS analyses use 1,000 replications per cell. For the NCHS application and the oracle precision diagnostic, the accompanying materials include the generating scripts, random-number seeds, monitoring grids, configuration, unit tests, and replication-level outputs, and document the steps needed to reproduce both analyses from the official public data sources. For the MODY-calibrated plasmode, the generating script and retained run summary are included. For Studies 1–4, the ancillary reproducibility archive includes the frozen numerical summaries used in the manuscript, the retained legacy scripts, and a clean reference implementation of the documented certification mechanics and configurations. Because the exact replication-level files and seeds from the final historical Study 1–4 run were not preserved, exact byte-for-byte regeneration of those displayed Monte Carlo summaries is not claimed.

Funding information

The authors report no dedicated external funding for this study.

Conflict of interest

The authors declare no conflict of interest.

Data availability statement

The observed-data analysis uses the publicly available US National Center for Health Statistics Cohort Linked Birth/Infant Death public-use files. The manuscript and accompanying materials document the cohort definitions, exclusions, sampling seeds, and data-preparation steps needed to reproduce the analytic samples. The MODY-calibrated analysis is a simulated plasmode and does not redistribute or analyze individual-level controlled-access genomic records.

Code availability statement

Code and simulation materials supporting the analyses are included with this preprint as an ancillary archive under the arXiv anc/ directory. The NCHS and oracle components include saved configurations, seeds, tests, and replication-level outputs; the Study 1–4 materials include the frozen reported summaries and a clean reference implementation of the documented certification mechanics and configurations, with the historical provenance limitation described above. The same materials will also be archived in a public repository upon journal acceptance.

Use of artificial intelligence tools

During preparation of the final submission, OpenAI ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol; accessed 28 August–1 September 2026) was used to assist with language editing, bibliographic cross-checking, consistency review, and review of code/documentation. It was not used to generate the research data reported in the manuscript or to make autonomous statistical or clinical interpretations. The authors reviewed the suggested changes, verified the mathematical statements, references, code, and reported results, and take full responsibility for the content.

Ethics statement

The analysis used publicly available, deidentified NCHS public-use files. No identifiable individual-level information was accessed, and no separate data-use approval was required.

Acknowledgments

The infant-mortality analysis uses the public-use NCHS Cohort Linked Birth/Infant Death file, which requires no separate data-use approval.
